name: Julius 'Jules' Ransom
languages: Muscogee Creek (a little, from the freedmen's families he grew up among in Oklahoma)
equipment: Derringer (Remington double-barrel), 2 rounds loaded, in the lining of his music case
His music case: pencil manuscripts, the band's piano book, and the score of 'Woodland Avenue'
A good dinner suit, ruined, and one patent shoe (the other was lost at Number Four)
Marked deck, which he does not use, and an honest deck, which he does
A gold watch that was his father's
A savings book from the Peoples Finance bank on Eighteenth Street with $612 in it
A photograph of Lavinia Ransom in a church hat, and her funeral card
Keys to rooms 3C and 3D at the Lincoln Arms and to a green-and-cream 1934 Terraplane in the police impound lot
features: Plain Dealing (Small-Town origin: once per long rest, advantage on an Insight check to tell whether someone is lying, and on a success, whether they lie to protect themselves or someone else; ordinary working people start one step friendlier)

The Long Con (Grifter: in downtime, a day and $20 builds a cover identity; he can keep 2; advantage on Deception, Performance and Persuasion to keep a cover up. He has never used it for anything but getting a band paid)

Cheap Shot (Grifter: once per turn, an extra 2d6 damage with a finesse melee weapon or a sidearm when he has advantage, an enemy of the target is within 5 ft of it, or the target believed a lie he told in the last minute)
Quick Hands (Grifter, 2nd level: a bonus action each turn to Dash, Disengage or Hide, or one Sleight of Hand check to lift, plant or palm something. This is how he took the book)
Racket: Roper (Grifter, 3rd level: a person he talks to for ten minutes treats him as a friend until given a reason not to, and will do a favor that costs them nothing without a check)
Ability Score Improvement (Grifter, 4th level: +1 Dexterity, +1 Charisma)

Back Room Game (Card Sharp background: he can find a card game anywhere in the city and read the players; he paid his way through his first five years in Kansas City at the card tables behind the clubs, and a dozen men on Eighteenth Street still owe him)

personality.traits: I am charming without trying and serious when nobody expects it. I hear everything as music: a car horn is an F-sharp, an argument is a call and response. I never raise my voice; I play louder.
personality.ideals: Nobody gets to use my mother. Not alive, not dead, not on a list in a window.
personality.bonds: My mother, Lavinia Mae Ransom, who scrubbed floors in Muskogee for twenty years to buy me a secondhand piano. The band. And Eighteenth Street, which took in a boy with a cardboard suitcase and made him somebody.
personality.flaws: I took that book because I was angry, and I did not think for one minute about who it would hurt besides Strode: Zora, Lucky, the band, every man in it whose name is in it. I am proud of what I did and sick about what it cost, and I would do it again.

appearance: A slim, handsome, brown-skinned man of thirty-three with a narrow face, high cheekbones, an easy crooked smile and long elegant hands he protects the way other men protect their eyes. When he is found he has a split eyebrow, two cracked ribs strapped tight and bruises the colour of plums; he holds himself very straight so that nobody will notice.
backstory: Julius Ransom was born in 1903 in Muskogee, Oklahoma, the only son of a railroad section hand who died when he was six and of Lavinia Mae Ransom, who cleaned houses and churches and saved for eleven years to buy him a secondhand upright from a Baptist church that was getting a new one. He played it every day of his childhood and at sixteen played it in a Tulsa dance hall, and in 1921 he was in Tulsa when the white mob burned Greenwood, and he walked out of it with his music case and nothing else and never talks about it. He came to Kansas City in 1925 with a cardboard suitcase, played the Lincoln Arms' lobby piano at four in the morning until a house detective named Matthias Hartsell was told to throw him out and sat down to listen instead, and by 1928 he had his own band. His mother came up from Muskogee to live with him in 1930 and kept house for him in rooms on Woodland until the house burned in 1931, and then in the Lincoln Arms, and she died at Wheatley-Provident in February 1935 with her hand in his. In September 1936 he saw her name in the window of Dandridge's Barber Shop, registered to vote at the lot where their house had stood. Everything since has followed from that.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Jules is the missing man and, once freed in bn-scenario-002, a companion. He is the campaign's moral centre but not a saint: he took the book in anger without thinking who it would endanger, and he knows it. Play him as charming, funny, proud and quietly furious, and badly hurt (in play he starts each scene at reduced hit points for the days he was held, per the Merry-Go-Round rule, and cannot play the piano with his right hand until about Tuesday; the sheet shows him healthy). He must never be a victim who waits to be rescued: in the cells he said nothing for a week, and that silence kept him alive and the book safe.
dmNotes.voice: Soft, quick, musical, a little Oklahoma left in the vowels. Talks with his hands even when they hurt. Describes people as instruments ('Strode is a clarinet: thin, sweet and nervous'). When he talks about his mother he is very precise, as if reading from a document.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: his mother's name off the rolls. Secondary: the book where it will do the most harm to the men who wrote it and the least to the people in it. Tertiary: the band, Thursday nights, and Chicago on the 12th for Geneva's sake.
dmNotes.secrets: He knows exactly what is in the book; he read it cover to cover in the band room in twenty minutes on Sunday morning, including the back pages and the initials N.V., and he did not understand what N.V. meant. Second: he survived Tulsa in 1921 as a boy and saw what a city does when it decides a Black neighbourhood is to blame; he understands the Monitor's headline in bn-scenario-004 before anyone. Third: he wants Strode alive, and is not entirely sure whether that is justice or revenge.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: gratitude, which he dislikes owing, and then real friendship. Toward Geneva: everything, unspoken. Toward Lucky: guilt for what he put in his trunk. Toward Quarterman: a cold, total contempt that softens, slightly, when he understands why. Toward Strode: he will play him a ballad if asked. Which one is his choice.
